perfidious

per-FID-ee-us · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Perfidious is deceitful and untrustworthy; willing to betray a trust.

Historians called the count perfidious after learning he had secretly negotiated with both sides of the war.

Example

The perfidious business partner signed a secret deal with a rival company the very week he promised loyalty to his own team.

Perfidious describes an intentional act of betrayal by someone who was trusted -- not a simple mistake or disagreement.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

treacherous: Treacherous is the everyday word for betraying trust, and it can also describe dangerous things, like treacherous ice on a road. Perfidious covers the same kind of betrayal but is formal and almost literary — the word you meet in history books and novels, not in everyday complaints.

faithless: Faithless means failing to keep a promise or a loyalty — a faithless friend simply lets the commitment quietly die, often through weakness rather than a plan. Perfidious is worse and more deliberate: a perfidious person actively schemes against the very people who trust him, while still pretending loyalty.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

loyal: faithful and devoted

trustworthy: deserving of confidence and trust

Where it sits · how deep the betrayal runs

unreliable → perfidious → treasonous

unreliable vs. perfidious: Unreliable simply means someone can't be counted on; perfidious implies active, intentional betrayal of trust, not just carelessness.

treasonous vs. perfidious: Treasonous goes further than perfidious, specifically implying betrayal of one's own country or ruler.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — per-: thoroughly, through (Latin)

root — fid: faith (Latin (fides))

suffix — -ious: full of, characterized by (Latin)

Put it together: per- ('thoroughly') + fid ('faith') + -ious together suggest going straight through someone's faith and breaking it -- the deep betrayal perfidious describes.

Use the root in a new word: confide: Confide shares the same Latin root fides ('faith'), joined here with the prefix con- ('with').
